This modest neonatal dimension suggests a high degree of maternal investment in yolk provisioning relative to body cavity volume, a pattern observed in several other xenosaurid congeners. The incubation period for this species, when maintained at a stable thermal regime of 22.7 °C [T = 22.7 °C], spans roughly 274.5 days [ab = roughly 274.5 days], a notably prolonged developmental phase that reflects the cool, montane environments typically occupied by Xenosaurus grandis. Adult females of this species attain a maximum snout–vent length of 12.5 cm [Li = 12.5 cm], a body size that is moderate compared to other members of the genus Xenosaurus but which confers a distinct advantage in terms of the volume available for developing embryos. Correlated with this ultimate size, the asymptotic wet body mass recorded for adult females is 23.4 grams [Wwi = 23.4 grams], a value that was estimated by scaling from the mass-length relationship documented in the related lacertid Lacerta agilis. This mass is attained gradually, as growth rates in X. grandis are heavily influenced by thermoregulatory opportunities in their crevice-dwelling microhabitats. The relatively large body size of reproductively active females is thought to facilitate the production of proportionally large offspring, which may improve juvenile survival during the first critical months following eclosion. Comparative data from other anguid and xenosaurid lizards suggest that this combination of modest clutch sizes and substantial neonatal mass represents a conservative bet-hedging strategy typical of k-selected squamates inhabiting stable but resource-limited environments.

Longevity in the Knob-scaled lizard is considerable for a reptile of its body plan, with the maximum lifespan documented under controlled laboratory conditions extending to approximately six years [am = approximately six years] when animals are maintained at 22.7 °C [T = 22.7 °C]. This extended lifespan allows individuals multiple opportunities to reproduce over their lifetime, partially compensating for the low annual reproductive output. After hatching, young lizards grow slowly, passing through several years of juvenile and sub-adult stages before reaching reproductive competence at around 32 months after birth for females and 28 months for males. Physiological studies indicate that the metabolic rate of this species is correspondingly low, a trait shared with other sit-and-wait foragers that occupy thermally buffered, structurally complex habitats like limestone crevices and boulder fields.

This protracted developmental delay of roughly 32 months is linked to the attainment of the minimum body size necessary for successful gestation. The earlier maturation of males is a common pattern in squamates and is thought to be driven by sexual selection favoring smaller, more nimble individuals that can effectively compete for access to crevice-bound females. Post-pubertal growth continues, albeit at a decelerated rate, with both sexes adding somatic mass incrementally until they approach their asymptotic dimensions several years later.

The thermal biology of this species is tightly coupled to its life history schedule, as all major developmental milestones have been characterized at a controlled temperature of 22.7 °C [T = 22.7 °C], which approximates the mean active body temperature recorded for free-ranging individuals in the cloud forests of Veracruz and Oaxaca. This conservative life history, characterized by low fecundity and late maturation, makes the species particularly vulnerable to habitat disturbance and adult mortality, as population recovery would necessarily be a slow process.
